topics: Community Nutrition Programmes and Nutrition Education in Ghana

questions.question_text: Which of the following nutrients is the body's primary source of energy under normal dietary conditions?

choices.text: Carbohydrates
Vitamins
Minerals
Water

questions.rationale: Carbohydrates are the body's main and readily available source of energy, providing approximately 4 kcal per gram. They are found in foods such as rice, maize, cassava, yam and plantain.

questions.question_text: Which nutrient is primarily responsible for the growth and repair of body tissues?

choices.text: Protein
Vitamin C
Carbohydrate
Water

questions.rationale: Proteins supply amino acids needed for tissue growth, repair and maintenance. They are also required for the formation of enzymes, hormones and antibodies.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is classified as a fat-soluble vitamin?

choices.text: Vitamin C
Vitamin B1
Vitamin A
Vitamin B12

questions.rationale: Vitamin A is fat-soluble and can be stored in the liver and body fatty tissues. Vitamins A, D, E and K are the four fat-soluble vitamins.

questions.question_text: Which mineral is an essential component of haemoglobin?

choices.text: Calcium
Iron
Iodine
Sodium

questions.rationale: Iron is an essential component of haemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that transports oxygen. Inadequate iron intake can contribute to iron-deficiency anaemia.

questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes a balanced diet?

choices.text: A diet containing only foods rich in carbohydrates
A diet providing all essential nutrients in appropriate amounts for an individual's needs
A diet that excludes all fats and oils
A diet consisting mainly of protein-rich foods

questions.rationale: A balanced diet supplies adequate energy and essential nutrients in appropriate proportions to maintain health and support normal body functions. The requirements vary according to age, sex, activity level and physiological condition.

questions.question_text: Which anthropometric measurement is commonly used to assess acute malnutrition in children aged 6–59 months?

choices.text: Mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC)
Head circumference only
Chest circumference only
Waist-to-hip ratio

questions.rationale: MUAC is a practical screening measurement for acute malnutrition in children aged 6–59 months. It helps identify children who require further assessment and nutritional intervention.

questions.question_text: What is the correct formula for calculating body mass index (BMI)?

choices.text: Weight in kilograms divided by height in metres squared
Height in metres divided by weight in kilograms
Weight in kilograms multiplied by height in metres
Weight in kilograms divided by age in years

questions.rationale: BMI is calculated by dividing weight in kilograms by the square of height in metres (kg/m²). It is commonly used to screen adults for weight categories, but it does not directly measure body fat.

questions.question_text: Which clinical feature is classically associated with kwashiorkor?

choices.text: Bilateral pitting oedema
Excessive muscle development
Increased subcutaneous fat
High body mass index

questions.rationale: Bilateral pitting oedema is a characteristic feature of kwashiorkor and may initially be noticed in the feet and lower limbs. Other features can include skin changes, hair changes, apathy and an enlarged fatty liver.

questions.question_text: Which feature is most characteristic of marasmus?

choices.text: Severe wasting of muscle and loss of subcutaneous fat
Generalised oedema as the defining feature
Excessive accumulation of body fat
Enlarged thyroid gland

questions.rationale: Marasmus is a form of severe acute malnutrition characterised by marked loss of muscle and subcutaneous fat. Unlike kwashiorkor, bilateral nutritional oedema is not a defining feature.

questions.question_text: Which nutritional deficiency is a major cause of nutritional anaemia?

choices.text: Iron deficiency
Vitamin D deficiency
Vitamin K deficiency
Excess iodine intake

questions.rationale: Iron deficiency is a leading nutritional cause of anaemia because iron is needed for haemoglobin synthesis. Other causes include folate and vitamin B12 deficiencies, infections and inherited blood disorders.

questions.question_text: Which condition is associated with severe vitamin A deficiency?

choices.text: Night blindness
Scurvy
Rickets
Beriberi

questions.rationale: Vitamin A is essential for normal vision, particularly in dim light, and for maintaining healthy epithelial tissues. Deficiency can cause night blindness and, in severe cases, xerophthalmia and corneal damage.

questions.question_text: Iodine is essential for the production of which hormones?

choices.text: Thyroid hormones
Insulin and glucagon
Oestrogen and progesterone
Adrenaline and noradrenaline only

questions.rationale: Iodine is required for the synthesis of thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3). Inadequate iodine intake can impair thyroid function and cause goitre and developmental problems.

questions.question_text: Which nutrient is particularly important during pregnancy for reducing the risk of neural tube defects?

choices.text: Folic acid
Vitamin K
Sodium
Vitamin E

questions.rationale: Folic acid is essential for DNA synthesis and normal neural tube development in the early stages of pregnancy. Adequate intake before conception and during early pregnancy reduces the risk of neural tube defects.

questions.question_text: For how long is exclusive breastfeeding recommended for most infants?

choices.text: The first 2 months
The first 4 months
The first 6 months
The first 12 months without any complementary foods

questions.rationale: Exclusive breastfeeding is recommended for the first six months of life. From six months, appropriate complementary foods should be introduced while breastfeeding continues.

questions.question_text: Which dietary modification is generally recommended for a patient with hypertension?

choices.text: Reducing excessive sodium intake
Increasing the intake of heavily salted foods
Avoiding all fruits and vegetables
Consuming unlimited processed meats

questions.rationale: Reducing excessive sodium intake can help lower blood pressure. A healthy dietary pattern should also include fruits, vegetables and other nutrient-rich foods while limiting highly processed foods.

questions.question_text: Which practice is most effective in reducing the risk of foodborne infection during food preparation?

choices.text: Washing hands with soap and safe running water before handling food
Using the same unwashed knife for raw meat and cooked food
Leaving cooked food uncovered throughout the day
Tasting food with the same spoon used for serving

questions.rationale: Handwashing with soap and safe water removes microorganisms that may contaminate food. Safe food preparation also requires clean utensils, separation of raw and cooked foods and appropriate cooking and storage.

questions.question_text: A community health nurse measures an adult's weight as 72 kg and height as 1.8 m. What is the adult's approximate BMI?

choices.text: 18.0 kg/m²
22.2 kg/m²
27.5 kg/m²
32.0 kg/m²

questions.rationale: BMI is calculated as 72 ÷ (1.8 × 1.8), which is approximately 22.2 kg/m². This falls within the normal adult BMI range of 18.5–24.9 kg/m².

questions.question_text: A mother at a CHPS compound asks when she should begin giving complementary foods to her normally developing infant. What is the most appropriate advice?

choices.text: At birth
At 3 months
At about 6 months
At 12 months

questions.rationale: Complementary feeding should begin at about six months because breast milk alone is no longer sufficient to meet all the infant's nutritional requirements. Breastfeeding should continue alongside safe, adequate and age-appropriate complementary foods.

questions.question_text: A pregnant woman attending antenatal care reports that she frequently skips meals because of nausea. Which advice is most appropriate?

choices.text: Eat small, frequent meals and choose nutrient-dense foods that are tolerated
Stop eating until the nausea disappears completely
Replace all meals with sweetened drinks
Avoid all sources of protein throughout pregnancy

questions.rationale: Small, frequent meals may help women manage nausea while maintaining adequate nutrient intake. The nurse should also assess hydration, weight changes and persistent vomiting that may require clinical evaluation.

questions.question_text: A pregnant woman at a CHPS compound is found to have low haemoglobin and reports fatigue and dizziness. Which nutritional advice is most appropriate alongside the prescribed management?

choices.text: Increase intake of iron-rich foods such as meat, beans and dark green leafy vegetables
Avoid all foods containing iron
Drink tea with every meal to improve iron absorption
Eat only starchy foods such as cassava and yam

questions.rationale: Iron-rich foods support haemoglobin production, and vitamin C-rich foods can improve absorption of non-haem iron from plant sources. Dietary advice complements, but does not replace, prescribed iron and folic acid supplementation or investigation of the cause of anaemia.

questions.question_text: A child has difficulty seeing in dim light and presents with dry conjunctiva. Which deficiency should the nurse suspect?

choices.text: Vitamin A deficiency
Vitamin C deficiency
Vitamin B1 deficiency
Vitamin K deficiency

questions.rationale: Night blindness and conjunctival dryness are important features of vitamin A deficiency. The child requires prompt clinical assessment because advanced deficiency can cause irreversible corneal damage.

questions.question_text: A community health nurse is educating households about preventing iodine deficiency disorders. Which recommendation is most appropriate?

choices.text: Use adequately iodised salt in appropriate amounts
Avoid all salt regardless of medical advice
Use only untreated sea water as a source of iodine
Replace iodised salt with large amounts of sugar

questions.rationale: Iodised salt is an important population strategy for preventing iodine deficiency disorders. Households should use iodised salt while still limiting total salt intake according to healthy dietary recommendations.

questions.question_text: A mother brings her 2-year-old child to a CHPS compound. The child has bilateral pitting oedema of the feet, sparse hair and skin changes. What is the most likely condition?

choices.text: Kwashiorkor
Marasmus
Obesity
Rickets

questions.rationale: Bilateral pitting oedema in a young child is a defining clinical feature of severe acute malnutrition with nutritional oedema, commonly referred to as kwashiorkor. The child requires urgent assessment and management according to the national severe acute malnutrition protocol.

questions.question_text: A 15-month-old child presents with severe wasting, prominent ribs, loss of buttock fat and no bilateral pitting oedema. Which condition is most likely?

choices.text: Marasmus
Kwashiorkor
Iodine deficiency
Vitamin A toxicity

questions.rationale: Severe wasting and loss of subcutaneous fat without nutritional oedema are characteristic of marasmus. The child needs prompt assessment for complications and appropriate nutritional rehabilitation.

questions.question_text: A community health nurse measures the MUAC of a 20-month-old child and obtains 11.2 cm. How should this finding be interpreted?

choices.text: It indicates severe acute malnutrition and requires urgent assessment
It indicates normal nutritional status
It indicates obesity
It is a measurement used only for pregnant women

questions.rationale: For children aged 6–59 months, a MUAC below 11.5 cm indicates severe acute malnutrition. The nurse should assess for bilateral pitting oedema and medical complications and arrange appropriate urgent management or referral.

questions.question_text: A community health nurse records the weight and length of an infant during a growth-monitoring session. What should the nurse do with the measurements?

choices.text: Plot them on the appropriate growth chart and interpret the growth pattern
Record only the infant's name and discard the measurements
Compare the infant's weight with that of an unrelated adult
Use the measurements to determine the infant's blood group

questions.rationale: Plotting accurate measurements on an age- and sex-appropriate growth chart helps assess growth over time. A child's growth trend is more informative than a single measurement considered in isolation.

questions.question_text: An older adult attending a community clinic reports poor appetite and unintentional weight loss. Which nursing action is most appropriate?

choices.text: Assess dietary intake, weight history, oral health and possible underlying illness
Assume weight loss is a normal and unavoidable part of ageing
Advise the person to stop eating protein-rich foods
Recommend skipping breakfast and lunch

questions.rationale: Unintentional weight loss in older adults may indicate malnutrition, oral health problems, chronic disease or other treatable conditions. A comprehensive nutritional assessment is needed before planning appropriate interventions.

questions.question_text: A mother reports that she gives her 4-month-old infant water and herbal preparations in addition to breast milk. What should the nurse advise?

choices.text: Continue exclusive breastfeeding without additional water or other feeds unless medically indicated
Give herbal preparations after every breastfeeding session
Replace breast milk with plain water during hot weather
Begin giving adult family meals immediately

questions.rationale: Exclusive breastfeeding means giving breast milk only, with no additional food or drink, including water, except oral rehydration solution, drops or syrups containing vitamins, minerals or medicines when indicated. Breast milk provides adequate water for a healthy infant during the first six months.

questions.question_text: A caregiver prepares complementary food for a 7-month-old infant using only thin maize porridge. Which recommendation would best improve the nutritional quality of the meal?

choices.text: Enrich the porridge with suitable protein- and energy-rich foods, such as groundnut paste or mashed beans, where safe and appropriate
Dilute the porridge with more water until it is almost transparent
Add large quantities of salt and seasoning cubes
Stop breastfeeding immediately

questions.rationale: Complementary foods should be nutrient-dense and provide adequate energy, protein and micronutrients. Enriching maize porridge with suitable ingredients improves its nutritional value, while texture and consistency should be appropriate for the infant's developmental stage.

questions.question_text: A mother says that her breast milk is insufficient because her newborn wants to breastfeed frequently. Which response is most appropriate?

choices.text: Explain that frequent feeding can be normal and assess positioning, attachment and signs of effective milk transfer
Advise her to stop breastfeeding and use water instead
Tell her that frequent feeding always proves that breast milk is inadequate
Recommend introducing solid foods immediately

questions.rationale: Frequent breastfeeding is common in newborns and helps establish and maintain milk production. The nurse should assess attachment, swallowing, urine output and weight gain before concluding that milk supply is inadequate.

questions.question_text: A lactating mother asks whether she needs to eat more nutritious food while breastfeeding. Which advice is most appropriate?

choices.text: Eat a varied, balanced diet and maintain adequate fluid intake according to thirst
Avoid all protein-containing foods
Restrict fluid intake to reduce breast milk production
Eat only starchy foods throughout lactation

questions.rationale: Lactation increases energy and nutrient requirements, so a varied and balanced diet supports maternal health and milk production. Mothers should drink adequate fluids and continue breastfeeding unless a specific clinical reason requires modification.

questions.question_text: A patient with type 2 diabetes attends a nutrition education session at a district hospital. Which meal-planning advice is most appropriate?

choices.text: Control carbohydrate portions and choose high-fibre foods such as vegetables, beans and whole grains
Consume unlimited sugary drinks to maintain energy
Avoid all vegetables because they contain carbohydrates
Eat large amounts of refined carbohydrates at every meal

questions.rationale: Carbohydrate quantity and quality influence blood glucose levels, so portion control and fibre-rich choices are important. Individual meal plans should consider medication, physical activity, nutritional needs and blood glucose targets.

questions.question_text: A patient with hypertension frequently eats salted fish, processed meat and heavily salted soups. Which dietary advice should the nurse prioritise?

choices.text: Reduce salt and high-sodium foods and use healthier seasoning alternatives
Increase the use of salt in every meal
Avoid drinking water
Replace vegetables with processed meat

questions.rationale: High sodium intake can contribute to elevated blood pressure. Reducing salt, limiting processed foods and choosing fresh foods can support blood pressure control alongside prescribed treatment.

questions.question_text: A patient with chronic kidney disease has been advised by the clinical team to restrict dietary sodium. Which food choice is most appropriate?

choices.text: Freshly prepared unsalted fish with vegetables appropriate to the patient's renal plan
Heavily salted dried fish and salted soup
Instant noodles with added seasoning powder
Processed meat with extra table salt

questions.rationale: Freshly prepared foods without added salt are generally lower in sodium than heavily salted or processed foods. Renal diets must be individualised because potassium, phosphorus, protein and fluid requirements depend on the patient's kidney function and treatment.

questions.question_text: A patient with liver disease and abdominal ascites asks why the clinician has recommended reducing salt intake. Which explanation is most appropriate?

choices.text: Reducing sodium can help limit fluid retention and accumulation of ascitic fluid
Salt reduction directly destroys liver viruses
Salt reduction permanently restores damaged liver cells
Salt reduction prevents the body from absorbing all nutrients

questions.rationale: Sodium restriction is commonly recommended in the management of cirrhosis with ascites because excess sodium promotes fluid retention. The dietary plan should be individualised to maintain adequate energy and protein intake while following the clinical team's advice.

questions.question_text: A food vendor at a community gathering prepares waakye and leaves it uncovered for several hours at room temperature. What is the main food safety concern?

choices.text: Microbial growth and contamination may increase the risk of foodborne illness
The food will automatically become more nutritious
Exposure to air destroys all harmful microorganisms
Cooked food cannot support bacterial growth

questions.rationale: Cooked foods left at unsafe temperatures for prolonged periods can support the multiplication of disease-causing microorganisms. Food should be protected from contamination and kept hot or refrigerated appropriately.

questions.question_text: A caregiver prepares fufu for a young child and uses the same chopping board for raw chicken and cooked vegetables without washing it. What is the main risk?

choices.text: Cross-contamination of cooked food by microorganisms from raw chicken
Loss of all carbohydrates from the vegetables
Improved food preservation
Prevention of bacterial multiplication

questions.rationale: Raw poultry may carry pathogens such as Salmonella and Campylobacter, which can contaminate ready-to-eat foods through shared utensils or surfaces. Separate equipment should be used for raw and cooked foods, or thoroughly cleaned and sanitised between uses.

questions.topic: Community Nutrition Programmes and Nutrition Education in Ghana
questions.question_text: A community health nurse identifies several underweight children during growth monitoring at a CHPS compound. What should the nurse do?

choices.text: Assess their nutritional status, counsel caregivers and arrange appropriate follow-up or referral
Ignore the measurements because children naturally differ in size
Give all children appetite stimulants without assessment
Advise caregivers to stop giving children protein-rich foods

questions.rationale: Underweight children require assessment of growth patterns, dietary intake, illness and household circumstances. Appropriate counselling, follow-up and referral help identify and manage malnutrition early.

questions.topic: Community Nutrition Programmes and Nutrition Education in Ghana
questions.question_text: A community health nurse is teaching caregivers how to improve children's dietary diversity using locally available foods. Which meal is the best example of a varied, nutrient-rich meal?

choices.text: Banku served with fish and kontomire stew
Plain cassava served with sugar only
Plain white rice without any accompaniment
Plain kenkey without fish, vegetables or other accompaniments

questions.rationale: Banku provides energy from carbohydrates, fish supplies protein and other nutrients, and kontomire contributes vitamins, minerals and fibre. Combining different food groups improves dietary diversity and overall nutrient intake.

questions.question_text: A mother brings her 3-year-old child to a CHPS compound because the child has poor appetite and has lost weight. Which action should the nurse take first?

choices.text: Assess the child's nutritional status, growth history and possible illness
Immediately prescribe a restrictive weight-loss diet
Tell the mother that weight loss is normal in all children
Recommend that the child skip meals until appetite improves

questions.rationale: Poor appetite and weight loss may indicate malnutrition, infection or another underlying health problem. A nutritional and clinical assessment should guide subsequent feeding advice, treatment or referral.

questions.question_text: A child with severe acute malnutrition is admitted to a district hospital with poor appetite, bilateral pitting oedema and lethargy. What should the nurse prioritise?

choices.text: Arrange urgent assessment and stabilisation according to the severe acute malnutrition protocol
Give a large high-protein meal immediately without assessment
Discharge the child because oedema indicates adequate nutrition
Restrict all fluids and food until the child gains weight

questions.rationale: Severe acute malnutrition with oedema and lethargy is a potentially life-threatening condition requiring urgent assessment and protocol-based stabilisation. Feeding must be carefully managed because affected children are at risk of metabolic and fluid complications.

questions.question_text: A school-aged child frequently eats maize porridge but rarely consumes animal-source foods, beans or dark green leafy vegetables. The child presents with fatigue and pallor. Which deficiency should the nurse investigate?

choices.text: Iron deficiency
Vitamin D toxicity
Excess vitamin A
Excess iodine intake

questions.rationale: A diet low in iron-rich foods may increase the risk of iron deficiency, which can cause anaemia, fatigue and pallor. The child requires appropriate clinical assessment and investigation because other causes of anaemia are also possible.

questions.topic: Community Nutrition Programmes and Nutrition Education in Ghana
questions.question_text: A community health nurse is planning a nutrition education session for households where many children consume mainly cassava and maize products. Which approach is most appropriate?

choices.text: Demonstrate how to combine staple foods with legumes, fish, eggs, vegetables and fruits available locally
Advise all households to stop eating traditional Ghanaian foods
Recommend that children consume only imported processed foods
Teach caregivers that food variety has no effect on nutritional status

questions.rationale: Nutrition education should build on locally available and culturally acceptable foods to improve dietary diversity. Combining staples with protein-rich foods, vegetables and fruits helps provide a wider range of essential nutrients.

questions.question_text: A breastfeeding mother asks whether she should stop breastfeeding when her infant develops mild diarrhoea. What should the nurse advise?

choices.text: Continue breastfeeding frequently and seek appropriate assessment if danger signs occur
Stop breastfeeding until the diarrhoea has completely resolved
Replace breast milk entirely with fruit juice
Withhold all fluids from the infant

questions.rationale: Breastfeeding should continue during diarrhoeal illness because breast milk provides fluid, nutrients and immune protection. The infant should also be assessed for dehydration and receive appropriate oral rehydration solution when indicated.

questions.question_text: A community health nurse obtains a BMI of 31.5 kg/m² in an adult during a routine screening. How should this result be classified using standard adult BMI categories?

choices.text: Underweight
Normal weight
Overweight
Obesity

questions.rationale: For adults, a BMI of 30.0 kg/m² or above falls within the obesity category. BMI is a screening tool and should be interpreted alongside clinical history, waist measurements where appropriate and other risk factors.

questions.question_text: A patient with diabetes reports frequently drinking sweetened soft drinks and eating large portions of white rice. Which intervention should the nurse recommend?

choices.text: Replace sugary drinks with water and discuss appropriate carbohydrate portions and healthier food choices
Increase sugary drinks to prevent low blood glucose at all times
Stop all meals and consume only water
Eat unlimited portions of rice because it contains no sugar

questions.rationale: Sugar-sweetened drinks can cause rapid increases in blood glucose, while large carbohydrate portions can make glucose control more difficult. Individualised meal planning should balance carbohydrate intake with medication and physical activity.

questions.question_text: A caregiver stores cooked soup overnight at room temperature in a warm kitchen and serves it to a child the next morning without adequate reheating. What is the main concern?

choices.text: The soup may contain increased numbers of harmful microorganisms or heat-stable toxins
The soup automatically becomes sterile overnight
Room-temperature storage prevents all bacterial growth
The soup loses only its colour but remains completely safe

questions.rationale: Warm room-temperature storage can allow foodborne microorganisms to multiply, and some organisms may produce toxins that are not destroyed by ordinary reheating. Cooked food should be cooled and refrigerated promptly or kept safely hot until serving.

questions.topic: Community Nutrition Programmes and Nutrition Education in Ghana
questions.question_text: A community health nurse identifies a pregnant woman who has limited access to food and is frequently missing antenatal appointments. What is the most appropriate initial response?

choices.text: Assess her nutritional and social needs and link her to appropriate maternal health and community support services
Blame her for failing to maintain a healthy diet
Advise her to stop attending antenatal care
Recommend that she take unprescribed appetite stimulants

questions.rationale: Food insecurity can affect maternal nutrition and access to healthcare, so the nurse should assess the woman's needs and identify available support. Linking her to antenatal care, nutrition services and appropriate social support can reduce nutritional and pregnancy-related risks.

questions.question_text: A child with severe acute malnutrition is found to have bilateral pitting oedema. The caregiver reports that the child's weight has not decreased. Which interpretation is most accurate?

choices.text: Oedema can increase measured body weight and conceal severe wasting or malnutrition
A stable weight proves that the child has normal nutritional status
Oedema always indicates excessive protein intake
Weight measurements are never useful in children with malnutrition

questions.rationale: Fluid accumulation can increase body weight and mask loss of muscle and fat in a child with nutritional oedema. Assessment must include examination for bilateral pitting oedema and other anthropometric and clinical indicators rather than relying on weight alone.

questions.question_text: A pregnant woman has fatigue, pallor and a low haemoglobin level. Her diet contains little iron, and she frequently drinks tea immediately after meals. Which explanation best accounts for a possible contribution to her anaemia?

choices.text: Low dietary iron intake combined with reduced non-haem iron absorption due to tea consumption around meals
Tea increases iron absorption and causes iron overload
Iron is not required for haemoglobin formation during pregnancy
Pallor is always caused by iodine deficiency

questions.rationale: Tea contains polyphenols that can reduce the absorption of non-haem iron when consumed with meals. Low iron intake and increased iron requirements during pregnancy can contribute to iron-deficiency anaemia, although other causes should also be investigated.

questions.question_text: A 3-year-old child has a MUAC of 11.0 cm and bilateral pitting oedema. The child is also lethargic and refuses food. Which interpretation and action are most appropriate?

choices.text: The child has severe acute malnutrition with danger signs and requires urgent referral or inpatient assessment
The child has normal nutritional status because oedema increases weight
The child has moderate malnutrition and should only return for routine growth monitoring
The child should be managed with unrestricted home feeding without clinical assessment

questions.rationale: A MUAC below 11.5 cm and bilateral pitting oedema indicate severe acute malnutrition, while lethargy and poor appetite suggest possible medical complications. The child needs urgent assessment and management according to the severe acute malnutrition protocol.

questions.question_text: A 9-month-old infant is fed thin maize porridge three times daily but receives no animal-source foods, legumes, fruits or vegetables. The infant's weight gain has slowed. Which explanation best accounts for the nutritional concern?

choices.text: The diet may be inadequate in energy density, protein and essential micronutrients
Maize porridge alone provides every nutrient in adequate amounts
Infants older than six months no longer require dietary fat
Slow weight gain is always a normal feature of complementary feeding

questions.rationale: Thin cereal porridge alone may not provide sufficient energy, protein, iron, zinc and other nutrients for an older infant. Complementary foods should be diverse, nutrient-dense and offered in age-appropriate quantities and textures while breastfeeding continues.

questions.question_text: A patient with chronic kidney disease is advised to limit potassium after laboratory tests show hyperkalaemia. The patient regularly consumes large quantities of bananas, oranges and avocado. Which dietary response is most appropriate?

choices.text: Review potassium-rich foods with the renal dietitian or clinical team and develop an individualised food plan
Encourage unlimited consumption of all fruits because they are natural
Advise the patient to stop all food intake
Replace the fruits with potassium-containing salt substitutes

questions.rationale: Hyperkalaemia can cause serious cardiac complications, and some fruits contain substantial amounts of potassium. Dietary modification should be individualised according to laboratory results, kidney function, medication and the patient's overall nutritional needs.

questions.topic: Community Nutrition Programmes and Nutrition Education in Ghana
questions.question_text: A community nutrition programme reports improved attendance at nutrition education sessions, but growth monitoring data show that underweight prevalence has not decreased. Which conclusion is most appropriate?

choices.text: Attendance alone does not demonstrate improved nutritional outcomes; the programme should assess feeding practices, food access, illness and intervention effectiveness
The programme has definitely succeeded because attendance has increased
Growth monitoring should be discontinued because education sessions are popular
The community should be blamed for failing to follow advice

questions.rationale: Programme participation is an output measure, whereas changes in nutritional status are outcomes that require separate assessment. Persistent underweight may reflect inadequate food access, infection, poor feeding practices or weaknesses in the programme's design and implementation.

questions.question_text: A 70-year-old man living alone has poor dentition, reduced appetite and progressive weight loss. He mainly eats tea and bread because he finds meat and vegetables difficult to chew. Which intervention is most appropriate?

choices.text: Assess for malnutrition and oral health problems, then plan soft, nutrient-dense meals and appropriate referral
Advise him to eat only bread and tea because they require little chewing
Recommend that he avoid all protein-containing foods
Assume that weight loss is inevitable in older adults and take no action

questions.rationale: Poor dentition and social circumstances can reduce food intake and contribute to malnutrition in older adults. Soft, nutrient-dense meals and assessment of oral health, swallowing, underlying disease and social support can improve nutritional care.

questions.question_text: Several people develop vomiting and diarrhoea after eating chicken prepared at a community celebration. Investigation reveals that the chicken was undercooked and stored at room temperature for several hours. Which conclusion is most appropriate?

choices.text: Inadequate cooking and unsafe storage likely contributed to foodborne illness
The illness was most likely caused by a lack of dietary fibre
Undercooked chicken is safer because it retains more nutrients
Room-temperature storage prevents the multiplication of foodborne pathogens

questions.rationale: Undercooking may allow pathogens such as Salmonella and Campylobacter to survive, while prolonged room-temperature storage can support microbial multiplication. Safe cooking temperatures, prompt refrigeration and prevention of cross-contamination are essential food safety measures.

questions.question_text: A 2-year-old child has severe wasting, bilateral pitting oedema and poor appetite. The caregiver requests that the nurse provide a large meal of fufu and meat immediately to restore the child's weight. What is the best response?

choices.text: Explain that severe acute malnutrition requires careful clinical stabilisation and protocol-based feeding rather than an immediate large meal
Provide an unrestricted high-protein meal immediately
Advise the caregiver to stop all feeding for several days
Discharge the child because traditional foods cannot be used in nutritional rehabilitation

questions.rationale: Children with complicated severe acute malnutrition may have impaired metabolic and physiological function and are at risk of complications during refeeding. Stabilisation and therapeutic feeding must follow the recommended protocol, with transition to rehabilitation when clinically appropriate.

questions.question_text: A child in a community with poor access to vitamin A-rich foods develops night blindness and Bitot spots. Which interpretation best explains these findings?

choices.text: Vitamin A deficiency is affecting normal visual function and the health of the conjunctival epithelium
Iron deficiency is directly causing all the eye findings
Iodine deficiency is causing damage to the retina
Excess vitamin C is producing the characteristic eye changes

questions.rationale: Night blindness and Bitot spots are recognised manifestations of vitamin A deficiency. The child requires prompt clinical assessment and appropriate vitamin A management according to national guidance because progression can lead to corneal damage and blindness.

questions.question_text: A patient with diabetes has frequent episodes of hypoglycaemia after taking prescribed medication but often skips breakfast. Which interpretation and advice are most appropriate?

choices.text: Meal skipping may contribute to hypoglycaemia; the patient needs review of meal timing and medication with the clinical team
Skipping meals always improves blood glucose control
The patient should independently double the medication dose
The patient should permanently avoid all carbohydrate-containing foods

questions.rationale: Some diabetes medicines can cause hypoglycaemia when food intake is delayed or reduced. The patient's meal pattern and medication regimen should be reviewed by the clinical team, and the patient should receive education on recognising and managing hypoglycaemia.
